conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with pregnancy, birth, and new motherhood. Today I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week, so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When we’re finished I’ll add up the numbers privately and we can talk about what they might mean and what next steps could feel helpful.

We’ll go one question at a time; I’ll ask each in everyday language, and you can answer however feels easiest. Ready to begin?

Thinking about the past seven days: overall, have you still been able to enjoy things or take pleasure in moments—whether it’s your baby’s smile, a favorite song, or a quiet cup of tea—or has even small joy felt hard to find?

It’s… it’s mostly felt hard to find. I’ll catch myself smiling when the baby grips my finger, but the feeling fades so fast—like I notice it, then it’s gone. Even that first cup of tea in the morning used to feel comforting; now it just tastes like something I have to finish before the next feeding.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, once or twice I sort of chuckled when my partner made a silly face at the baby, but it felt forced. Mostly I just feel flat, like I’m too tired or heavy to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Hardly at all. I used to get excited about little plans—like a walk to the coffee shop or a phone call with a friend—but now when I think ahead it just feels… empty. I tell myself “maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like it,” but that spark never really shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If he spits up right after I feed him, I immediately think I must’ve done something wrong—maybe I held him wrong or ate something that upset his tummy. When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. this week, I kept replaying the day in my head, convinced I’d missed some cue and that a “good mom” would’ve known how to keep him comfortable. Even little stuff, like forgetting to switch the laundry, makes me feel like I’m failing at everything.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep in the bassinet and my heart’s still racing, checking every five minutes to make sure he’s breathing. Sometimes I even imagine these awful scenarios—like what if I trip on the stairs, or what if the ceiling fan falls on him—and I can’t shake the pictures in my head even though I know they’re unlikely. It’s like my mind keeps spinning worst-case reels even when everything looks perfectly fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a few times—maybe three or four days this past week. Out of nowhere my chest feels tight, like I can’t get a full breath, and suddenly I’m sure something terrible is about to happen even if the house is quiet. I’ll rock the baby faster, pace the hallway, keep peeking out the window to check… nothing. It passes after a bit, but each time leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning a little. I’ll finally get him down for a nap, look around at the dishes, the laundry, the bottles that need sterilizing, and I just want to sit on the floor and cry. Sometimes I manage to tackle one thing, but the rest keeps piling up, and I keep thinking, “How does anyone do this?” I haven’t used any wine or pills to cope—just push through until the next feeding, the next diaper change, the next cycle of exhaustion.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening a lot. I’ll lie down once the baby’s finally asleep, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” and the guilt, and suddenly it’s two hours later and I’m still wide awake. Even when I do drift off, the slightest whimper from the bassinet jolts me awake, and then I can’t settle again. I’d say maybe four—or five—nights this week I’ve spent more time staring at the ceiling than actually sleeping.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me from the moment I open my eyes. I’ll be feeding him and tears just start sliding down my face for no clear reason. I feel heavy, like I’m moving through thick fog, and even when I try to tell myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, we’re safe—it doesn’t lift the sadness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a few times this week. Once was when he wouldn’t latch and I felt like my body was failing him; another time was when I dropped a clean burp cloth on the floor and just couldn’t bend to pick it up again. It’s not sobbing all day, but the tears come quickly and feel like they’re right under the surface most of the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. I get exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he needs.

You've shared how the joy that used to come easily now slips away almost as soon as it appears, and each day feels wrapped in a heavy, gray fog. Despite cherishing your baby's tiny fingers, you're carrying constant worry, self-blame, and a sense of drowning in ordinary tasks, all while sleep remains frustratingly out of reach.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no spontaneous laughter, describes forced chuckling and feeling flat, matching "Not at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes loss of anticipatory pleasure for even small activities, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for everyday infant issues and household tasks, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, worst-case scenario thoughts despite objective safety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic episodes (tight chest, dread, pacing) occurring multiple times, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily emotional drowning, inability to manage household tasks, and frequent tears—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to distress, occurring most nights this week.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, tearfulness, and emotional heaviness, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by minor stressors, indicating crying is "quite often" over the past week.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to key <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day (Q8,9), markedly diminished interest (Q1,2), fatigue & worthlessness/guilt (Q3,6), sleep disturbance (Q7), and anxiety features (Q4,5). A score of 26 far exceeds the ≥14 cutoff for urgent referral. Combined with peripartum timing and functional impairment, findings strongly suggest probable moderate-severe <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within one week
2. Discuss evidence-based treatments: individual <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist partner/family for split night-time shifts to secure 4-5 hour continuous sleep block
4. Provide 24-hour crisis contacts: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, local emergency department
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening  
Date: [today]  
Responder: 4–6 wk postpartum mother, partner present, infant well  

A. EPDS Item Review (0–30 range)  
Estimated raw score ≈ 18–20 (items 1 & 2 = 1; items 3–9 = 2–3; item 10 = 0) – above routine cut-off for major mood concern.

B. Symptom Endorsements  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Daily guilt / self-blame, “not a good mom” cognitions (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety, intrusive catastrophic images, panic episodes (Q4, 5)  
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to ruminative worry, not infant alone (Q7)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, inability to complete tasks (Q6)  
- No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan (Q10)

C. Observed Patterns  
Symptoms present “nearly every day” × ≥ 2 wks, cause functional impairment (household tasks, social withdrawal), not better explained by substances or medical issues per respondent.

D. Screening Risk Factors  
- Postpartum period < 6 wk  
- Primiparous, history not reported  
- Lack of restorative sleep  
- High self-criticism & maternal guilt  
- Anxiety comorbidity (possible postpartum anxiety disorder)  
- Denies suicidal ideation (documented) – current safety risk low

E. Summary  
Screening findings are consistent with significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms, warranting prompt formal evaluation for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and/or Anxiety Disorder due to general medical condition (postpartum). Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for diagnostic interview and treatment planning; continue routine pediatric / OB follow-up; provide emergency contacts.
